blocks.x: This is September the 25th and it's an interview being recorded in the Howard Tilton Library, Seminar Room 2, Tulane University. Okay. Oh, and I better put my name on here. My name is Dick Allen.
What's your name? Prince Miller. Mine is Prince Miller.
Okay. Fine. Well, let's start up where we left off. Seems to me we were just getting you up to Chicago.
Yeah.
What happened when you got up to Chicago, Prince?

Well, I went in there with a big show from traveling on the road in the year of 1927. And the show was named the Miramak Miramakers. And after I got in Chicago, well, I struck all, struck luck there with fellas like Al Wynn, Tiny Palm, and Hughie Swift and all them kind of fellas. And I just got good there and made good. So I just stuck on, got to blowing around there. Got up together with a little fella called Francois Louisanans. He had been trying to get a band up together. So we worked together, say about five or six years, more than that. We worked at the Golden Lily five straight years. And the place caught a fire on a Saturday night, so that closed that job. But we still went on, playing different spots, swing lane.
Well, to get back to the, you're getting there, you were playing with Miramaks, Miramakas? Miramakas. Now who was the Bronze Bannikens? That was the same album?
No, that was Charles Taylor.
And when did that come?

Well, I started in that, I say, I don't know, the time, things got kind of slow there in Chicago, and I went out on the road with them. See, it must have been around, it wasn't in the 40s, before the 40s.
Was it before World War II?
Or 39 or something like that, huh?
Was it before World War II?
Yeah, a little before that, a little before that.
Well, that gives us a rough idea. Yeah. Now let's see. When you first got to Chicago, what was the first band you played with, other than Miramakas?
Well, the first band I played with was with, I see Al Wynn, he had a little band at the Dreamland.
Uh-huh. At the Dreamland, huh? Who was in the band?
Well, I don't know, me and Cliff Jones on drums, and some other guys, I can't remember them fellas now. Been a good while, you know.
Was this the same band that made the recordings?

No, no. Every time they make recordings, it's a couple of different bands, you know. One place I worked, I never did get to tell you, where I was doing very good, a place they called it the Bookstore, on 35th Street. It would open say twelve o'clock at night, and catch all the performance from all nightclubs and things, see. They called it the Bookstore, but they sold, you know, whisking stuff and things like that. But they did sell books in the front, and we had a little four piece outfit in there, and we just did good every night, every night. Had a lady on the piano, Ted Williams' wife, Irene her name was, and she the one supposed to have the little outfit, see. Well that's the time that Junior Cobb's come heard me play, and he's working out of South Chicago and Jeff with Huey Swift. And he come and heard me play that night, and I went back and told Huey about it, so Huey, he come on back and heard me play, and wanted me to join that big band out there.
What was the name of the club that Huey Swift was in?
It was the Jeffery Club, South Chicago and Jeffery.
I see. Now, you were first with Al when, and then with who?
I went to the bookstore, I told you. The bookstore? Yeah. And then Huey Swift? Yeah. That's right.
I got it, I see. And how long were you with Al when? Well I say a little more than a year or something. And how long were you with Irene Wilson, I guess her name was?

Yeah, Irene Wilson. Well we stayed at the bookstore about a couple of years, you know. Couple of years. Yeah. And I went with Huey Swift out there and worked over there three or four years, but the federal people closed that place. I don't know what was wrong, something was wrong there. And they closed it up, let's close it completely up. So that's the time I went with this Francois Louisianans.
Well that's all very confusing to me because there's too many bands. Like, you worked with Tiny Palm some, didn't you?
Yeah, but this was a little after this.
Well that was after Huey Swift? Yeah. And after Francois? Yeah.

Tiny Palm was after Francois? No, Tiny Palm was a little before Francois. See, I don't know if it, I don't know if it was Tiny Palm Band or Al when band, but they both was there together. See, you know, I think it was Tiny Palm, but Al when was doing a lot of managing, you know. But I'm pretty sure it was Tiny Palm Band, see.
Where at? At the Dreamland in Chicago. That's your first job on then?

Well yeah, I had a first job I went on in Chicago outside of the Miramac Miramaker show. Yeah. We was working at the Monogram Theater, but I was Dublin. I would leave there and go into the Dreamland right across the street, see, and play there with them. Yeah. So it sort of had two leaders in, really, huh? Well yeah, Al when was doing the hiring, I know that, he hired me. Mm-hmm. But Tiny Palm was writing all the music and taking everything else. How big a band was that? Well then they had something like twelve pieces. Mm-hmm. Yeah, they had big bands then.

Was that when you made the recordings with Palm? Yeah, yeah, same time. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. So, uh, you might have had some of the same men on the Palm records that you had on the Al Wynn records. That's a possibility.
Yeah, yeah. All be out of the same band. Yeah, this Hopskin fellow, he was using two trumpets then all the time. And he was there still all the time, see. He was Tiny right-hand man.
Yeah, I see. Now, the drummer though was Snaggs, you say, huh?
Yeah, Snaggs was the drummer.
Yeah, why?
While I was there, I know you were. Mm-hmm. Yeah.
Did you ever work with Errol Hines?

Well, no, not, I have worked in his spot, you know what I mean, like this. See, they went off, and we taking their place for a few days. We was a little Louisiana band I had. Mm-hmm. We had, and until they come back, then they went back on the job. But I never worked in his band. Mm-hmm. Tell no lie about it.
What about Dave Payton? Did you ever work with him?
Yeah, I worked with him at the Regal Theater when it first opened up. Mm-hmm.
And who, which other bands were you working with while you were working with Dave Payton?

Well, to tell the truth, I was still with the Lusianans. Mm-hmm. But Dave Payton was just getting up a, what do you call it, something like an all-star band to make a big opening there, see. Mm-hmm. And he made that big opening for two days, Saturday and Sunday I think it was. All day Sunday and Saturday night. And then after that he had got his regular band, you know, what he wanted there, but I was still with Francois Lusianan. Mm-hmm. Yeah. I see. So, how many years were you with Francois? Well I'm going to be straight with you. I'm telling you, I stayed with him longer than I did any band in Chicago, I know that. Mm-hmm. He was a little band, we were just all boys from New Orleans, you know, we just stuck together, just like that. Mm-hmm. And how we broke up was when the place caught a fire and Francois was the type of fellow that didn't finally get around and look for nothing, see. Mm-hmm. So the boy just coming to scatting, you know, and getting different jobs and things. And Francois, he went on a run on the road from Chicago to Los Angeles. So I worked with everybody then. Well, who was everybody after you left Francois? Who was some of the people? Well, the fellow that I really can't, I haven't called their names right now, but they had little old four and five pieces, you know. Mm-hmm. Of course I had little outfit there once myself, I was on Madison Street there. Six pieces out there, working from McDonald's. And I worked there until I was taking six, you know, I was taking six from whiskey. And after that, that's when I gave up.
What year was it you took sick? Do you remember?
Yeah. Yeah. This was in forty, forty, one I think. That's when I quit drinking. Yeah, that's forty-one. Mm-hmm.
Forty-one. Well, I was wondering about it, Pontch. Let me fix that machine there. When were you in Springfield? Right.

Well, I was there with a fellow named Oliver Bibbs. That was late after, way after me and Francois and them broke up. That's where I must have been in. It must have been around thirty, oh, not no thirty. Around about, 45 or something like that. 46, 47, around that day. Long after you'd stopped drinking then. Yeah. Oh yeah, I quit drinking altogether.
Was the war going on there? Right after World War II. Right after World War II, I see. I see.
Well, that was a good job. Mm-hmm. That was Sidney Bichet, the fellow that had been playing there, and he went overseas, and we took his place.
Well, let's see. Now, let's see. Sir Oliver Bibbs, how many jobs did you play with him? Play many places with him?

Yeah, I worked Silhouette Club with him, and I worked at Garrick Bar with him, and I worked at Club Rio with him, and I worked at, what was it? Martin's Condor. Martin's Condor. Mm-hmm. On the west side with him. That's in Chicago. Oh yeah. Oh yeah. Oh, Chicago. And that Silhouette Club is a beautiful place. On Harvard Street. Well, when did you first start going on the road then? When I left with Miramac Miramacos. First trip I took.
No, I mean after you were in Chicago. Huh? After you were in Chicago. Well. Things started getting slow, you said.

That's what I said, and this fellow come through with them Brown Manigan I told you about, Charlie Taylor. Mm-hmm. Well, he hadn't heard of me a long time, so he come up to a place where, well he used to work with Miramac, and then had Miramac Miramacos when he first started out. So he had his own show, and he come up and asked, what was I doing? I told him nothing, so he asked me how would I like to make a trip with him. Mm-hmm. So I got with them and went on the road with them, and I must have stayed with them for three years, see. Mm-hmm. Three years. And to tell the truth about it, I have never exactly lived in Chicago no more since then, because when I quit them I went to New York, from New York I got on the road again, then I started trying these carnivores shows. Well that killed it right there. The Royal American, the different O'Connells, I can't call the name of them now, but six or seven different ones, every summer you know. Dress up in the winter, go somewhere in some town in the wintertime and play around, and then go back on the road with them again.
Well that's the thing most that killed me up. Well now, who did you work with in New York?

What did he work with? His name's Stone. The last name is Stone. I can't think of his first name. What did he work with? I was to make piano, I was to make records with him, and the same show, see how I got to New York, when the carnival closed, Charlie Taylor was the man who had the brown mannequin. He said, Puncher, never lived in New York, no time, why don't you come on and go up there with me and stay with me, just you know, just winter, until I get ready for my show to go out and then we'd all come out together. Well I went on there with him, see, and that's when I went to playing them jam sessions, and making records, that's when I made them records, Ho Ho, Ho, Ho, and then. Yeah. That's the time I made them records, and I lived at his house in New York, so I got this fellow, Stone, I'll tell you about, I think his first name. He called me a pretty full time, told me when his job was going to start, when he was going to make records and everything, and Charlie Taylor got ready to go out on the road, well I just dropped all that, went on the road with Charlie Taylor, see, again. But I wish I would have stood there, if I stood there I would have stood there right, see. Stone, his name is some kind of Stone, he's a good piano player, good musician, he had a band in Chicago a while.
I can't think of who that would be. His name's Stone, anybody tell you.
Guy Kelly, and Red Carey, you heard of him, Carey, played saxophone. Red Carey? Yeah, you never heard of him either?
I can't place him, I'll play him.
Well they played with Stone band in Chicago, all them guys, he had a nice band there man. And then he left Chicago and went to New York see, and stood around they playing.
Who else did you play gigs with in New York?
Well just fellows, boy white boy played piano, was his name?
He made the records with you, is that the one?

Yeah. Ralph Sutton. Sutton, yeah. I played with him, tell the truth, the whole time I was in New York, because everything I got he called me up and I'd go on with him, even Harvard Connecticut and all out there I went with him.
I see. So, you went, after New York you went on with these carnivals.
Yeah, I went back on the road.
And first were the Bronze Mannequins, and then when? And then who were some of the others?

Well, now I'm going to tell you, the Bronze Mannequins, this year he played the Heaney Brothers. And they shared he had two calls, he put one band over on the Heaney Brothers and one band on James C. Straits. Well I'd manage this band, some other fellow managed that band. Well I still would try to tell you about four years, but he sent for his brother and gave his brother a show, and he was such a wild catcher, you know, couldn't nobody get along with him, so I just quit my whole outfit. After about three or four years I'd been with him, see. Then I joined a man called Jerry Jackson, from Nashville, Tennessee. He played the Cavaliers show. I worked with him about a couple years.
What instrument did he play?
He didn't play, he just do the booking and manage the show and things.
Any New Orleans guys in those bands?

No. Then I went with this show called The Royal American, that's the biggest show on the road, I played with them three years. I left them and went to Silas Green and played with him two and a half years, after that, see. When I left Silas Green, well, I went to Jimmy Straits with a fellow named Scotty, a great drummer, that's when I left him and come on to New Orleans in 56. Got Scott taking him, he was getting sick, he wanted me to stay up there, but I stole it off from him. The fellow was leaving, coming to Memphis in his car, and I just got in the car and come on to Memphis, and him from Memphis I grabbed the train and come on to New Orleans, I've been there ever since.
When did you get here, what year?
The last part of 56.
And let's see, that fellow Crawford.
It was in October, November, October.
Remember this fellow Crawford, the photographer of Ralston, he took your picture when you were with Silas Green, right? Yeah. Up in Mississippi.
Yeah, sure did.
Yeah, well we'll check the date on that, he'll have the date on that picture. Let me see now, so you've been here, and who have you worked with?
Well I just had a little outfit here myself, since I've been here. I haven't been doing much playing, I work more as I, the work I did more of that here since I've been here.
That reminds me, all those years on the road were you working days at all?
No, no, no.
So you haven't worked days until you got back here.
That's right, that's right.
When was the last day job you had before you came here?
Hmm?
When did you have a day job before you came back to New Orleans?
When I was on the farm at Richmond, Louisiana.
Yeah, never, that's fantastic to go all those years without working. Just play music, huh?
That's all I did.
So you come back here and you've had a few jobs, that's right, I can remember a few of them.
Mm-hmm. Let's see, you've been on television.
Oh yeah. How many times were you on television? Just once, yeah. Just once, that's one time. Yeah.
And let's see, ever make any movies? No, I never make no movies.

I heard once they grabbed us picture in Chicago, they're playing at the Howard Street, they're playing at the Howard Street, they're playing at the Howard Street, they're playing at the Howard Street. I've seen the people around there doing all that work but I didn't think they could take
nothing else. But they said they did, they said they had us in a picture, I don't know. Of course if we know that we could have got paid for it, that's when I didn't believe it.
Have you made any records since you've been back here? Not here, no. Not any real band records or anything? No. Well you made that thing with Sam I was just telling you about.

Well yeah, but I didn't know anything about that, so Sam got to let me know something about that. But I'm really planning on if I get a little more strength making something like that, because I got some good stuff, I'll sell it all out, I'll do something with it. But of course I've got to wait a little while, yet I'm trying to rush myself up a little too fast. I've just got to wait a while.
Did you ever work with Doc Cook? Yeah.
Wife of Memphis?
Well Doc Cook had a band in Chicago, Charles L. Cook?
Oh no I didn't work with him. I know you're talking about, they had one on the road too, Doc Cook.
Oh now that's a different guy.
Yeah, yeah. I know you're talking about now.
Ever worked with Jimmy Noon?
Yeah, I played with Jimmy Noon. Not study, but I played jobs with him you know.
Where was that?
In Chicago. I worked at Tipus Inn with him. Worked white club with him a couple of nights like that.
White club?
White club, sure. On the west side.
Well what about the pay in all these different years? How was the pay down here in New Orleans when you first started?
What do you mean pay money?
Yeah money.
Oh when I first started?
Yeah.
Well let me see, I believe the first job I got in New Orleans I got something like two and a half with Jack Kerber.
Now before that in Raceland would you make any money?

Oh yeah we'd make, like, me and this boy they called Lonnie Johnson now, we called him Rooster at home, but we'd play on Saturday evening on a big store gallery you see, and put our hat down and all the people that's playing put money in our hat see, we didn't have no siren or nothing like that. But when we got through, that Saturday and that Saturday night, that Saturday evening and that Saturday night, we ain't gonna have enough money to lend us all that next week. See? Yeah.
Just play that one day and you'd have enough to make it all.

Saturday, it's all day Saturday and Saturday night and we might play a little guitar, bass and trumpet outfit for something about white folks you know on Sunday night like that. But how much would that pay? Well that pay us like about two dollars a man.
How much would you get for those tips on Saturday?
Oh, them tips run around about fifteen dollars, something like that. That'll last a long time.
Oh yeah, in those days. In Chicago you told me about making real good money with Tiny Palm.

Yeah, I made good money with Tiny Palm and I made my best money with Oliver Bibbs. So Oliver Bibbs, I made the best money with him. I got ninety, eighty-five dollars, Tiny Palm, but I got a hundred dollars flat every week with this Oliver Bibbs.
What about somebody like Francois when you had those five years?

Well we wasn't making, but I'm going to tell you how that worked. I might as well come clean now it's over with. We was playing for a chairman and he couldn't pay the right salary, see. But to hold a job, the chairman was supposed to pay us ninety dollars a man a week. But he said he couldn't pay. He could pay seventy dollars a man a week. But we would get the ninety, but each man had to go to Francois and throw back. And that money Francois would bring it in to him Sunday night and give it back to him. But we held a job like that five years, see. But we wasn't getting paid no ninety dollars, we were getting paid seventy.
Well that was tough times too, huh? Yeah, oh yeah. Well that was wonderful money I guess for the Prussian years all through those years.
Yeah, well we pretty much was doing pretty good all the way through that. That's the truth.
Well times got better in a hurry for you I guess.

Well, I made my little mistakes myself in Chicago. I was doing good but I got a little, you know, whiskey and stuff. Got ahead of me. I didn't never use dope in my life. But I was a whiskey drinker. I said, never have used dope in my life. I guess that's the reason I'm still here, because if I had been using dope too I would've been gone. I just couldn't see that. I could see my whiskey though.
Now how'd you make out with carnivals? Did they pay well? Those little shows?
Yeah, but take up all your money to live on them carnivals.
How much would they pay a week?

Well they say seventy dollars a week. You got a birth, you sleep in a birth, they're going to take out for that. You got to eat with them, they're going to charge you like the devil on that train eating, see. And you got to pay big money for your food, your cigarettes, your smoke, see. And when you finish up you're making about forty dollars a week, I don't want to call it, when you finish paying out of everything, you know what I mean?
That's the same for Mac, Billy Mac, and the same for Solid Screen and American, whatever you want.

All that's the same, you make good salary but the money would go, you have to let it go for your living expenses, you got laundry and all that stuff, they don't pay for nothing for you, you got to pay for everything. Mm-hmm. For yourself.
What about, uh?

Well one thing I like about the Royal American, every time you go out with them, they pay the same money, but when you start, the day you start to wake, you're boneless start. And when you get back and go in, you got a hundred and fifty dollar bonus. Your salary would be like four to five dollars a week, after taking expenses out. Well if you can save any of that back and you get back and put that hundred and fifty with it where you got you something. I know fellas come back and have six hundred dollars, six hundred dollars, something like that. The best I ever did was five, I come back with five, one year.
That was for one summer, you came back with five hundred dollars?
Yeah.
Well you did all right, I never did that well.

Yeah I did all right that summer. And Solid Screen show, how I got lucky there, they would gamble every pity. Played what you call strip poker, they played it hard too, but heavy. And I'd lose my pity, heavy pity I'd lose. So a couple of weeks there, something got ill, me and I got lucky, and I wanted me about seven dollars, about three hundred dollars this week, about three hundred dollars next week. So I just banked all that in the bottom of my trunk, I wouldn't touch it, I'd leave it on my side until we come in. I come in that year, about four hundred and something dollars. That's by me saving it, you know.
What's strip poker like? How do you play that?

Well they call it loose deuces. But it's strip poker, like they deal you five cards, and you got three aces, and maybe you got a seven or eight, where you put your three aces down and throw them in. And everybody, what they don't, card they don't like to throw them in, well they give you two more cards. But on them three aces, if you catch another ace, you got a great big hand. You sure have. Four aces, see. And if you catch two kings, well that's a full house, you see. Three aces and two kings.
Well they call that draw poker, right? Yeah. Same thing as draw poker.
Yeah, same thing as draw poker.
Now what is cotch anyway?
Cots, well I'll have to sit down and show you that. That's a peculiar game. You take the tens out of the deck.
Clean out.

But you use two decks. See, the little end of the deck, the ace is the one, deuce is two, three is the three, four is the four, five, five, six, six, well that's the deck. Right there. You dig in, the seven is the ace, the eight is the deuce, the nine is the three, the jack is the four, the queen is the five, the king is the six. And then you deal from the bottom of the deck. You don't deal from the top, deal from the bottom. And men can play with a little small deck like that. But the reason of it, so many men are going to get out, you know, pass out all the time because they ain't got no kind of card. You catch a deuce or something like that, you ain't got nothing there, you see, so you just throw that in. Men get a five spot and a six spot, and a man may bet on a four.
Does it work like poker? Is it similar to poker at all?
Well, it's on the order of poker, yeah, but it's not different.
Well if you had four deuces, would that be good in cotch? In cotch?
In cotch?
No. What do you got to have to win in cotch?

Well, they go by numbers. If you got six of hearts, and five of hearts, that's eleven. That's a big hand. Then if you catch the four of hearts, or the three of hearts, or the deuce of hearts, or any other kind of hearts, you got cotch. That's called cotch, that's the name of the game, cotch. If you catch three sixes, that's the biggest cotch in the deck, three sixes.

We'll have to get a deck of cotch, a couple of decks, and we'll cotch. We'll come back and play sometime. Yeah. You can show me how these different games work. Yeah. Tunk is another one I want to play.
You don't know Tunk even?
I never have played Tunk, man. I wish I had a deck of cotch.
Or Coom Can, I've never played Coom Can. Yeah, Dick get a deck, yeah?
Yeah, we'll get us some decks, and we'll learn how to play those games, because I think all that, people ought to know that, you know?

Yeah, and something else I'd like for you to know right now, Dick, of course this ain't supposed to be on here, but I can say so. We got to move right after the first of the month. They're going to repair that house. Yeah. And I think, of course I'll let you know where it is, but I think we're going to be down on Second Street there somewhere, but I'll have to let you know later.
You'll be near Carrie Boots. Huh? Right near Carrie Boots.
Somewhere in New York, yeah, we're closer than we are now.
Yeah, well, I'll check with you, Coom Can. Yeah. Well, let's see. We're just sort of rambling on about different things now. Now in New York, did you make good money?
Yeah, I wasn't in New York, but I was in New York, it must have been like three months. And I worked the whole time with stuff stuff
there. The whole time I was there, I was waiting.
Did you have any steady gigs there?

Yeah, that's what I'm talking about. Gigs was with the Sutton fellow and made records, and then they called me for that jam session down on 2nd Street. Where they called? I believe it was, I don't know New York City. 22nd, eh?
I don't know, Stuyvesant Casino?
I believe so.
Let's see, they used to have-
Kept it every Sunday they have jam sessions there.
They used to, well there's Jimmy Ryan.
Across the street from the Deucers.
From the Three Deucers?
Yeah.
Gee I don't know New York that well. Now there's 52nd Street.
Yeah well, I believe that's the street.
And they have Ryan's there, Jimmy Ryan's.
That's the place, that's the place, Jimmy Ryan's.
And they used to have Sunday Afternoon's there?
That's right, that's the place. I never could think of the name of it, Jimmy Ryan's, yeah.
Well who was their steady band there?
Well they had a band that played there, but I don't know who they were, they wouldn't be there on Sundays.

Yeah, Wilbur the Paris is working out now. Is he? Yeah, you know Simeon died, huh? How long ago? Oh it's just been a, he went in the hospital on Labor Day and he just died about a week ago. Well I didn't know that, see that? Maybe ten days, almost Simeon died. I didn't know that.
See all that hits me man, just, when I hear things like that, this boots me off.
Well when I saw him, he was, had a real hoarse throat, you know, I guess it was at Canton there.
Where, in the throat?

Yeah, cause he, you know he was talking real hoarse and we had a few drinks together, you know. God, that's awesome. Well I wonder how does that feel? Will it be so? I don't think it just your voice gets hoarser and hoarser. Yeah, well mine do that.
No, you don't sound like him.
I mean it really gets much worse than that. Oh yeah. And uh, I don't know, I think you start bleeding you know and spit up blood.
Boy, boy, boy, I'm telling you. Well that's the end of this tape. Well, I tell you what I do, I run, I run, take a leak right there, that's all.
Okay. Okay, it's going now.
Okay, Dick.

Let's see, you remember where we left off? I think we were just talking about things in general. Yeah. So let's get back to what happened at Larry's now. You used to work there in the art gallery, huh? Yeah.
Playing music.
Yeah. How did that work now?

Well that worked out nice, we got a little light salary, but the tips was the main thing. And we made real good tips there. Real good tips. And uh, there's a little funny thing about it. This is something I had to get after, but I got to tell it. See when I had the white boys there waiting with me, well they didn't want any money. All the money went to me. All the tips went to me. But when I got to the place where I had to use the other boys, well then I had to start splitting up you know. So that made it much different. Made it much different. And about going to jail, well that was one of them nights the giant was jumping. I mean it was packing jamming. The policeman walked in, told us to quit playing. We quit playing and told us to come on outside, went on outside and took us on down. But it wasn't nothing to it. There was me coaching the next day. And it was all over with, because that judge did some talking there.
But they just dropped everything after the talking. Yeah.
There was no more to it after. And that was when you sang that song the next night.
I remember that. You remember? Yeah, but the judge don't order them to explain it.
Yeah. Well let's see, who was there? In the band? Yeah. Yeah.
There was one. And wasn't that the fella who used to play the sticks?
He didn't have no drums. The guy you have a picture of at home?
Yeah, he was there.
Fergie, yeah. That was Ferguson. And Charlie DeVoe. Yeah, and then they had the banjo player from Wisconsin.
Yeah. Joe Oltzalter and his Brady. And Kit Thomas. Yeah. He asked Kit Thomas a lot of questions.
And he knew Kit Thomas. Yeah, you know better than that, don't you?
Yeah. Boy, that was funny, I'm telling you in a way.
And they had that drummer named Doggy.
I can't remember.
He was there.
He was there.
And the guy you have a picture of at home? Yeah, he was there. Fergie, yeah.
Yeah. And then they had the man from Wisconsin.
Yeah. And then they had the man from Wisconsin. Yeah. And then they had the man from Wisconsin. Yeah.
And they had that drummer named Doggy. I can't remember his name now. Uh-huh. That's what my mom. But a lot of us used to come there.
Yeah. Well, I mean, Dick, where you was that night?
I had a headache.
I always know you'll always be there, you know.

Well, that night I just didn't feel like coming. I don't know. I couldn't get with it, you know. I had a headache. Uh-huh. But I got away. I always miss it so far. They never had to take me to the jailhouse. Yeah. Well, he wasn't taking me.
He said he'd never seen this thing before in his life.
Well, they didn't take Erwin in. I believe they did.
Or he got out of there or something.
I don't know. You know who was playing? Joe Lodd was playing piano that night. And he didn't have any horn with him, you know. He wasn't playing trumpet.
Oh, yeah.
Yeah. And he just walked out. They couldn't catch him, you know. Yeah. Joe told me about that.
I think the only white boy was with us in that coat was Charlie. Charlie, wasn't it Charlie?
Charlie and the two boys.
Yeah, two more boys.
Two boys from Wisconsin. Yeah. Joel Salter and Doggy. I think Doggy's name was Burger. And they, let's see, they had Ewan, Eddie Morris, and Kent Thomas.
Yeah.
And I missed that lecture from the judge myself. I wasn't there.

Boy, he did some talking. He told Ewan, say, what you people doing up there? You can't do it here. He said, they're trying to do it to us, but before, the only way they do it, they got to ram it down our throats. I don't need this now, no. I shouldn't take it. I just take so much medicine. I always want to take something. There ain't nothing bothering me now. I ain't going to take it. Let me sit there. Okay.
Well, you do need it.
Yeah. And that's the way that come off.

Well, let me get out my little notebook again, Punch, and we'll go back and I'll ask you about some of the different people and bands you work with, stuff like that. I wanted to ask you more about the different styles of the trumpet players they had here. Like, how would you describe Buddy Petit's style?

Well, I'm telling you, he had a wonderful style of playing at home. He wasn't a high note man, but he was, he had a wonderful tone and played everything clean. Real clean trumpet player. He was. Rene, he was a high note man. He went up in the air all the time. Ricard was turning out to be a nice trumpet player too until he got hype. Ricard was getting all right. What about Chris Kelly?
How did he play?

Well, Chris was a nice man with a plunger, you know. He was a plunger man. Yeah, I know. Well, I'm going to tell you how this happened. When I first came here from the Army, somebody carried me down to 25, where Louis was playing. And I got up there and played two numbers over there and some other song I played. And oh, that's the, let me see what, no, Kid Olive wasn't there. There's Kid Orange, Johnny Dots, Baby Dots, Lorenzo Stahl on guitar, and Bob Lyons on bass. That's how it was. And I played them two tunes and got to kidding Louis about it. Louis got mad boy. I told him, you take him, I'll just go ahead on, let's take him on in the band. So they said, oh no man, we're just kidding. So from then on, I just said, Louis was a great little trumpet player, he was younger than me though. But he was crazy about me playing. I was working at that storage, you know, when I got a job. And he had to go to the boat out on the river there. And he'd get right across the street up there and watch up there and be playing for hours before he'd go to white. Way back when he'd get ready to go. He's crazy about my playing.
Well was Louis copying anybody at that time? Did he have his own style already?

I think he did. Tell me one thing he did, he always had his own style playing, but what he did do, the stuff that he got famous with, he took it right from here. All the stuff that he, you know, heebie jeebies and all that kind of stuff. Well he got that from, I sure the boys was playing that up in the streets here, but they didn't know what he was doing, you know. And Louis just went up there and made something out of it, see.
I see. Well who did Buddy Petit play like? Anybody today or any other record jammer?

Well I've been trying to figure that out. Buddy Petit had a style, just was hard to get into, you know. I can blow a lot like him, but I just can't keep his style up going, cause he could go way down and get them pedal notes, you know, bring one of them, diminished chords and things and all like that. He could play a real good horn.
Was Joe Oliver doing anything like him at all?
Joe Oliver?
Mm-hmm.

Well, I believe he got something out of it from Joe Oliver. That's a fellow I never did know could do, Joe Oliver. And the first time I seen him was when I went to Chicago. I didn't never see him down here. First time I saw him. I went to Chicago to the plantation one night, the whole show went out and I went with him. And that's the first time I seen King Oliver.
Was there any of the guys playing like Freddie Caput down here?

Well, no. But I played with Freddie, you know. That's something I forgot to tell you. Now that was a trumpet player in the band. See, I went to that dream and there were so many different fellows, but now I went there with Freddie Caput. But how it happened, it wasn't tying the band to Freddie Caput band. Oh yeah. But I went there with him.
Who was in the band with Freddie?

He had some boys there, a light boy on tenor. And I'll tell you who he had with him. Lester Boone. You remember him? Yeah. Alco player, tenor player, something. Well he had him, and he had Felipe Trombo from here, Dutre, what's his name, Noda Dutre or something like that? Noda Dutre. Well he had him, and me, and himself, and he had a violin player named Clowns Lee. He was a good violin player, boy. He was a sweetheart. He played the devil out of the violin. And them the ones I can remember. I don't know if he had Snaggs on drum or not. That's the only drummer I remember. I played with a whole lot in Chicago with Snaggs. Francois, he played a drummer in that little band. I played with him with Snaggs, I played with him more than any drummer.
Well along the subject of drummers in Chicago, ever remember Andrew Hillier?
Sure I remember Andrew Good. Who was he with? He died, didn't he? Yeah. Yeah, we used to call him Hillier, yeah.
Who did he work with?

Well, I'm trying to think. I think he worked a whole lot with Dave Peyton. Yeah, he's up there along in that class, Dave Peyton. He worked a whole lot with Dave, I know. He worked a whole lot with Dave Peyton.
Yeah. Now, those trumpet players, let's start comparing some more of them to get that style down, if that helped you. Let's see. You see, nobody played much like Keppert, huh?

Well, Keppert was a rough fellow. He could hit them hard notes rough and quick, you know, like that. He played nice horn, but I mean, when he hit something, he just hit it hard and heavy. That's what he told me. He said, he always hit it hard. Don't blow it easy, hit it hard.
And, you know, he was a nice. Now, did Bunk play anything like him?

Well, Bunk was a nice trumpet player, but he played different from Freddie. Bunk was a good, solid, regular trumpet player, you know. That's the most man I think Buddy Petit got ideas from, Bunk. I think Buddy got right close to Bunk.
What about Lee Collins? How did he sound?

Well Lee, he's on the order of Louis. He likes Louis playing, you know, and he plays more like Louis. But he's right from here, you know, he's got the same southern style, but he's got a whole lot of Louis stuff.
Now, who had the outstanding reading bands here in New Orleans when you got here in 1919?
Well, Joseph, they tell me, did a lot of reading in the tuxedas.
Joseph who?
I can't call his name, I couldn't call it for you. He's down there on, on, on, first of the living room, I got a barbershop. Oh yeah.
There's a, there's a, there's a, John Joseph was the name.
Yeah, John Joseph from there.
He's a bass player. Uh huh. There's Nelson Joseph and, uh, Kaiser was there.

Kaiser, played the clarinet, didn't he? Yeah. Oh yeah. And they had a tall fella in the band. He was a good resistance. He was a reader. I think he played violin, but I can't think of his name. Well, let's see. I don't think he was in no relation to them.
There's a guy named Robichaud, John Robichaud was a violin player. No, John Robichaud, no. A.J. P. Rohn, Peter Boccage. No, none of them.
Paul Dominguez. A brown skin fella. Paul Dominguez.
I can't think of any other more violin players offhand.
Well, he was one. He was a good one too, but he lived uptown. All them you talking about, they lived downtown, was it?
Uh huh, yeah. They had that.
I can't, but I'm going to get somebody to tell me that guy's name.
Yeah, well. Did they have many good violin players when you got here?
Well, all I know is EJ, and Peter Owen, and Roe Bishore, and that fella you just called, Bocard or something.
Peter Bocard. Yeah.
He plays trumpet now. Yeah, them fellas. Them the only violin players I know.
Paul Dominguez. Did they uh?
I found that fella they'd be insane in them games. Such as? Hmm?
Such as? Such as?
Hmm?
Such as?
Yeah.
Such as which clarinet players?
I said like uh, George Boyd and Zeb, what's his name, Zeb?
Zeb, yeah.

And uh, he played with Rennie and this guy played with Bocard Petit, he's downtown now, way downtown there. That beats me. Yeah, he got a house down there, he don't play much now. You ask Raph about it, Raph took me to his house. Raph knew him good. He lives downtown. Way downtown, yeah.
Well we'll ask Raph.

Yeah, you just ask Raph about it because, I mean I went down there with Raph and he was supposed to make up, we were supposed to get together but I never did hear from him no more. I can't call his name. Can't call his name to save my life. But he from way downtown there. Was he look like? Used to be a good kind of player with all his teeth out in the front.
Tall, dark fellow. Well that'd be to me, we'll figure out who he is. Mealy Barnes.
Mealy Barnes, that's him. Oh sure. That's him, Mealy Barnes. And who did he work with? He worked with Buddy, and Buddy, Buddy,
Well I was hoping you could get together with him.
Well that's what I thought too, but.
Well he never did get any jobs done on him. He quit playing music.
He was worried about that house, you know, getting his house built. Mealy Barnes, yeah that's the fellow.
But he worked a lot with Buddy, huh?
Yeah, man.
But who had the straight bands, you know, straight reading bands other than.
Well Robichaud and Tuxedo did a lot of reading. But after that, them other fellows, they weren't doing much reading. This Desveen fellow too, he had a nice reading band.
Sidney Desveen.
Sidney Desveen, yeah.
And those guys, would they play any jazz at all?

Yeah, they play jazz, but it wasn't the hardest to hit musicians, you know. Yeah. It looked like they had something in them, they'd just take it all, take all, all that stuff out, that music stuff, they'd just knock that out. No fire.
No. Did they have any blues singers here in the old days? No.

Willie Jackson. I don't know what that fellow's name, Snooki Scotty or something Scotty. Them was the only two singers. I knew what they were around here in them time. Snooki Scotty, huh? No, his name was Willie Jackson and Colin. Yes. He worked there, right down there, right there, right there where, Tom Allison used to be right down below Canals Street, right in the block there below Canals Street. That place there now, what do you call it? Big old- Woodworth. Woodworth there, no, yeah.
He works at Woodworth, huh?
No, he used to work there for the, for the, for the, Tom Allison. There was a nightclub right there on that corner.
Was he Willie Jackson's partner?
Yeah, there was Snooki Scotty or something like that.
Yeah, well I know who that is, I can't think of his name.
Yeah, they was buddies, yeah. Yeah.
Any women singing?
I can't remember none, not in them times, way back there, I didn't remember no women singers.
Lizzie Miles, did you know her?
Well, that's, yeah, but that's Lizzie. She's gone, I guess. Yeah, she was gone.
I mean she was gone when you got here, huh?
Yeah, she's out of town, she wasn't around here then. I didn't know her until I came back here, you know. What about Ann? She went up the country a long time, didn't she?
Oh yeah. What about Ann Cook?
Ann Cook? She wasn't no singer, was she?
Yeah, she sang with Louis Delaney on the record.
She was after I left here, yeah. But Ann Cook was a hustling woman, I know her.
Well, she's a singer now, a church worker, you know, a big woman in the church.
That's good. Well, that's all I heard.
She was a nice quiet kind of lady, huh?
Yeah, she was.
Bust your head by her.
She had some terrible brothers too.
Yeah.
So she was quiet, you think? No, I'm only doubting you. Oh, I thought so, because Ann Cook was terrible. Yeah.
She's quiet now, but she must have been something in her day.
Yeah, she was a rough cat. Where's she living now, I wonder?
22, 27 Thayer, I think.
Uh huh.
It's in the phone book.

Yeah, she, last time I seen her, she's right across the street from that club there on Clio in Saratoga. What do you call that? It's a night club there, little old night club there. That beats me, I can't remember. Yeah, well, she's living right across the street from her. I stayed there one night.
Well, she's on Thalia Street now.
That ain't full of front of them. Yeah. Did they have many solo piano players that you knew of? In them days?
Uh huh. Well, the piano players that I didn't know, they all were pretty much waiting for me.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Nobody stuff with stuff Now Steve, he was with P-Rone, and Robichardt a piano player at the Lyric Theater. And Miss Todd used to play with the Tuxedos. Well now they had a big band, but all the rest of them bands used with five pieces and you had no piano.
Well who were some of the piano players you knew then who were working alone or with

a singer? Well Mr. Todd, I know Steve Lewis with P-Rone, and Miss Kimball was with Robichardt, and his wife and his husband played trumpet, Kimball and Miss Kimball, and she played the piano. Well them was about the only ones I know, you know, piano players. They had guys used like Pichon, well he always had a job by himself in the clubs you know, Walter Pichon, you know him. Yeah.
I just wondered who some of the ones that were in the district here, you told me you worked
with them. Well there were a lot of them in the district, I didn't know the name, playing blues and things by themselves. There were lots of them around in there. Yeah.
You said you worked once with a piano player I think somewhere.
Oh yeah, at Toodleums? At Toodleums, yeah. Yeah, what I'm saying now, at Blues Phil.
Yeah, you don't remember his name by any chance.
Yeah, his name was Willie Smith, but he dead.
Yeah.
Well. Willie Smith.
Good to know.
Yeah. Yeah, I worked with him there.
Let's get a little more on Wilbur Parrish, the drum hall player. When did you go with him?

He joined the Miriamak Miramaker show. To tell the truth, he come here with him when I joined him to New Orleans. He was with him. And I played in theater with him, see. And they asked me to come on and go away with him. And I just had gotten married too, but I explained it to my little wife, what to do when you're in the way. I told her after Lent I'd come right on back. But I went on and joined that show and went on up to Chicago and that was it, see.
That was when you went to Chicago. 1927 with that show.
I left here with that show. And who was the band leader then? Huh?
Who had the band in charge?
Wilbur.
Wilbur had the band in charge.

Yeah. And that's the fellow I told you I made something on my own and he wrote it down for me to play and I couldn't play. The same fellow. Who else was in the band? Do you remember any of them? Hemingway.
What did he play?

Piano. I'll tell you about him. James Hemingway. James Hemingway. And bass and all that. I really hadn't forgotten now, he was changing up so much. But I know they had a little fellow down on the drum named Buck. He was here a long time, stayed in New Orleans a good while. Bucket they called him. And Popeye on Alto. I can't call them guys names now that I wanted. But the guys was with him.
Did you ever hear Eva and Thomas and Bunk play together?
I didn't know Eva and Thomas.
You never heard Eva and Thomas? Oh Eva and Thomas.
Yeah.
Yeah.

I didn't hear them play together, but I remembered him one time because we played at Lafayette, Louisiana. I went with old Andrew Foster when I had my little band. And Eva and come up there, he wasn't playing that night, but he come up there and played something for me. He was a straight horn player, strong, but wasn't a, you know, not a whole lot of flesh. He was a straight, strong horn player. I see.
Who was this Foster fellow? What Foster?
I mean George Foster. No, Andrew Foster you just said.
Oh he was the guy who used to take bands out.

He didn't play nothing, but he'd go book days and things, come in and get bands and take them out, see. Big star, dark fellow. That was your band then? Yeah, that was my band then. Why did they call you the Iron Man?
That's what some of them used to call me. What did that mean? It mean I was strong, powerful.
I see. Did they have the same kind of dancing in Chicago they used to have down here? When I first went there, yeah, they was doing the same thing. Same thing.
I see.

But one thing I will say, I don't know, the Chicago people when I first got there, they liked it more blues numbers like. Because Duke Ellyn was playing nice sweet stuff and things and they kidded him. But when Louis went there with all that jumping and clowning and all kind of felt like me, you know, and the other people went for that, crazy about that. But later on they got to going for that nice music, you know. Later on, yeah, they got to going for that classic stuff. Later on.
Do they have more shows in Chicago than here, or more here?
Oh yeah man.
Lots of comedians and dancers on the stage and all that.
Yeah, now that's a funny thing, Dick. They used to have a lot of chorus girls and comedians and things here. They ain't got that no more. Here? Right here.
Where did they have that?
Well these guys used to have practices or have teachers teaching them how to dance and things going here. But they don't have that no more, yeah.
But where did they work? I mean, what clubs?

Well they had, let me see, they had the E-Lights. And then you know, like every time they play a big dance they have a floor show in different halls and they have floor shows and they have girls out there dancing and going on. And the theaters, they was working in the theaters often, see. But they don't have none of that no more. I mean, but one chorus girl, yeah, nah, nah, please tell me she done left. Nah, she gone to Memphis. Her name was May Bell. And what about comedians? Who were some of the comedians? Well, this fellow with Dodge, not some time back. I know his name, Poplar. Yeah. I can't think of him. They got ice cream names, just like him. Is it like Lollipop Jones? Lollipop, Lollipop. Lollipop Jones. Yeah, he's from here.
And he did a lot of clowning and everything in the old days.

Yeah, and this little fellow named Memphis. Memphis. And they had a little, you know, a little guy named Memphis. I heard some people say he wouldn't, but I heard he was from here. He wrote some more. Yeah, he got ice cream names, just like him.
Is it like Lollipop Jones?
Lollipop, Lollipop. Lollipop Jones.
Yeah, he's from here. And he did a lot of clowning and everything in the old days.
Yeah, and this little fellow named Memphis. Memphis. And they had, what do you name, I ever wrote that song, Sarah Martin Sings. Cox, Jimmy Cox.
Was he from here?
Well, nah, that's what I heard. And I heard some people say he wouldn't, but I heard he was from here.
He wrote some good numbers. You know, he wrote Nobody Knows You When You're Dying in the House.
Yeah, he wrote Last Go Round Blues.
Yeah, a whole lot of things like that he wrote.
Yeah, he wrote some. And he had a good voice too.
I never heard him on a record.
Boy, he had a good voice. Yeah, I don't believe he made a record, did he?
Not that I know of.
No, because he wrote this song, On His Dying Bed. Sarah Martin sang it.
Last Go Round he wrote On His Dying Bed.
Hmm?
He wrote Last Go Round On His Dying Bed.
Yeah, Last Go Round Blues.
What about Tom Benton? Did you ever work with him?
Yeah, he worked with him and Jack Carey Band. He was a banjo player.
Did they have many odd homemade instruments and stuff like that when you were coming up? No.

The only thing they used sometimes was a fellow could play a good alto, you know like playing brass band? Well they'd throw him in the jazz band if he could play it good, mixing that with us, you know.
Who would that be?

Well they had a fellow Yard, forget that boy named him now, he used to play in most all these bands, that alto. Even him was Oscar. Oscar something. Oscar Devone, Oscar Devone, Oscar Devone, some kind of Oscar or nothing. But he could play that like that alto because he'd sit down and work with us lots of times. It helped out a whole lot. Like I said, we'd let you rest. Yeah. Did he play melody?
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Did he play melody?
Yeah.
Well what would you play?
Well I'd take down when he'd play.
Yeah. He'd just swap, aren't you?
I'll tell you how he'd do, when we all opened up like that he'd play off, you know, play side melody, see. And then if I'd take down and say I'd jump on the lead, see.
Well that ought to sound pretty good. Sure it did. I've heard Ricard play a little melody on an alto horn sound pretty nice. I can't think of many of those guys like that I know.
No, that meant all these instruments come out here in Italy man. It worked out when I first started.
Well what about washboards and homemade stuff?
Oh yeah, all that was out there. Yeah, these boys up and down the street with them. All in the country.
Who would be some of those guys?

Well there was one guy that I called Sing and Shine. Sing and Shine. He could sing good, play guitar good. And he kept a little outfit like that with him all the time. Tub, washboard, and a pipe, pipe horn. You know, pipe horn.
Well how did that work?
Well good that guy played it.
He got a lip on it like a trumpet or did it have a reed on it?
He just had a round pipe. He'd go boop, He played it too.
Did he have a slide or? No. No, no. Just a round pipe.
Round pipe. About how long? About that long.
Three feet long. Yeah.
And he'd hold it right down, hold it like that you know. And he could make, it sounds like he's in tune all the time to me.
If he did that with his lip, that's something.
Not so loud, but you could hear it though. Yeah. Well he went all over. Smiling, smiling, Shine went all over with that man, all over the country with that.
What about the harmonica players?
Well, they had some good harmonica players too, but they wasn't in bands though them days and times. Like they all know.
Yeah, what would they do, just walk around?
Yeah, the harmonica would play by themselves you know.
Serenading and strolling huh?
Yeah. They wasn't in no bands.

Let's see, what are some of those other things that they had like that? They must have had some more instruments. Hmm? They must have had some more instruments. What about mandolins? Did they use mandolins in their jazz bands?
Well, I never did play with a mandolin. I beat it with a little head of my time. But they used to play in bands though.
They used to have them in bands.
Yeah, but I never did play with nobody to play a mandolin yet.
Would they have a mandolin and a horn too? Or would it just be all strings?
I think all strings.
I see.
Guitars, violin, mandolins, and bass like that.
Did you ever see any mandolin players you remember?
Yeah, in the home of Louisiana I went one time to play on Excursion. I seen them with a violin and a mandolin and a guitar and a bass playing. And it sounded very good. Did you know them?
No, I didn't know them.

I didn't know them. That's the first time I've seen a bunker. I was in the country then. I was a little boy then, but I was playing music. And I went on Excursion to home in Louisiana and I stood by a bunker all day long, man. That's not even blow.
Who was he playing with? His own band? Yeah, his own band, yeah.
Bunker Johnson.
Did you ever locate Evelyn Carey?
Yeah, she come to the hospital one day. Oh, yeah. So, she sure did. You know where she's at? She gave me her address. Nah, I got it somewhere at home at the house.
Oh, we'll have to find that, man. That's Jack's daughter, I mean.
Yeah, that's Jack's daughter.
And I was wondering.
Well, I can find out easy. Yeah, good. I know where to find out.
You told me one time about a guitarist being Poison. You don't remember his name, do you?

No, I can't think of that boy's name now, but he was a nice looking, brown-skinned kid. Lot of girls around him all the time. And he was a good, good guitar player too, but I don't know what his name is now.
What about this trumpet player that got paralyzed, you remember? One time you told me, Poison, about this woman told a man that if he hit her, he'd never use that arm anymore. Oh, yeah, that was.
I've forgotten his name too, but I knew he got a paralyzed stroke.
Where did he live, that guy, you know him? That well?
He was in, I think he's from Mississippi. Oh, yeah.
Yeah. He wasn't a New Orleans guy then? No, no.
I see.
Okay. How come you left New Orleans to go to Chicago?

Well, I think it just was the idea of, I was after a little money. I wasn't making enough anything. People were all bragging about how people from here was going to Chicago, doing good, in New York, cleaning up, making big money, and I just thought I'd get on up there and make some of it too, which I did. I did.
What was the main reason for people leaving the South in those days? Leaving New Orleans?

Well, my idea was, take a fellow like Joe Oliver, one of them who left first, and they were just writing back, telling the other guys how good it was up there, you know, and going on like that, and first thing you know, another one, he done left, and later on, and the others done left, and they all just went up there and started making goods, see. That's how it happened.
I see.
And that's just, just the way all that went.
Well, did they have much segregation in Chicago?

Well, I'mma tell you, about the spots, take on the south side, because there wasn't no segregation. But, it wasn't much as deep on the west side, but right in the heart of town, they like the loop, they call it. It was segregation, it's like anywhere else. Yeah, it was. What about in New York? You know, this is bad.
This is bad. You think living is better in those days in New Orleans, or New York or Chicago?

Well, I thought you had a little more, you know, a little more different, better up the line, a little better, you know. But I still say they had a few precious places there. And anybody that knows will tell you that.
Mm-hmm.
Yes. They take right out of Chicago there, like Whiteings, Indiana, and all them little town, man, were just as precious as they could be. Yeah.
Well, then where would you say the best places for colored people would be, as far as segregation is concerned and everything?

Well, I liked it candidly, pretty much, if you want to know. Of course, I didn't find a bit of difference there. Everybody seemed to be alike there to me. And a little town right here in this country I went to, it was a mighty nice town called Des Moines Highway. I stood there pretty good while. That was mighty nice.
Who were you playing with when you were in Des Moines?
I was playing with a little bunch up there with, well to tell the truth, I was the same fellow Oliver Bibbs. Mm-hmm. See?
And who went to Canada? When I went to Canada?
Yeah, who were you playing with?
I was at the Royal American show then.
Big Royal American show, we'd go there every year.
And people treated you pretty nice, huh? Oh, yeah.
Yeah, you don't mind, you ain't got time to look at you. See?
Well, what's the worst place you ever been in? I think the worst place I've been in my life is waiting in Indiana.

Worse than Georgia, Mississippi? They're going right. You couldn't, you didn't have to hire an automobile or nothing in Georgia or Mississippi to go through there. They might get after you or something, but you didn't have to hire. But in Whitings, Indiana, if you was in an automobile, and any kind of white man in there, you'd have to hire. Get out in there and hire and do something to go through there. Whitings was just that bad in them times. And they said, just that way of yet. The boy was talking about it yesterday. They're just that bad right now. Whitings, Indiana. Well, what would they do to you? And they ain't got a near-color family that live there, near one. They can work there, but they gotta get on away from there.
What about, what would they do to you in Georgia, Mississippi? Do you have any experiences with them?

Well, no, I'm gonna tell you the truth. No, because I've never had no trouble in places. I always was, you know, stayed where I was supposed to stay and kept in the right places, you know, where I was belonging. I never did mingle up in places where I had no business, you know what I mean? I was telling them one insult I remember getting one time, that was in Florida though. I was expecting a letter from this fellow I used to work with, McBride. And, you know, I told him just write to the post office and I'd go get it. And I went there to ask for a meal. And some white guy asked me, nigga, where are you going? I told him I'd come to ask for a meal. here. I said, well you just wait there and tell this white people get from around here and then you come on in, we'll let you on in. Well that's the only place I've had any trouble. They didn't do me nothing, but that's just the way they spoke to me, you know.
Well did any of the guys you know ever get in serious trouble, say, you know, down

behind the sun as we say? No, one boy named Charlie Calloway, we was playing, I was playing with the same shooting, this happened in Atlanta, Georgia, was it? Yeah, Atlanta, Georgia. And the white guy was drunk, you know, he kept on buying him, kept on buying him, he was selling Coca-Cola, you know, around him, and all the white folks, he didn't keep on following the boy around. Who was selling Coke all the time? Charlie Calloway, colored boy, he was the MC on the show, but before the show go on, you know, to sell Coke and candy and all that. And he said, well he just kept on until he got married every hard way and hit the boy. So the boy just jumped on him and whipped him. Just whipped him up good. Well nobody said a word. And when the law comes, they take Charlie Calloway, all the white folks got up to him, you know, that boy was right. So the men kept on buying him, kept on wood, and peeking at him all the time. Calloway whipped the white guy. Yeah, whipped him up good. And he didn't bother Calloway, told him to go on and go to the white, took him and made the white man get away with him. Didn't come to jail, but he made him get away from around there. But he was really wrong, that fellow was. He just kept on after that. Say, remember that Blue Island Blues you made
with Tony Parham? I think I played it for you one time. Yeah. What was the Blue Island?

Well that was, uh, there was a place on there called Blue Island. Did Tony work there or anything? Yeah, Tony worked there. But I wasn't really. I see. But it's a place called Blue Island. Yeah, that's way out south in Chicago, Blue Island. Yeah. Was it a nightclub or a town? It's a town,
but there were two, three nightclubs in there. Oh, I see. Did you ever work any jobs with Big Bill?

No, I just made records with him. I see. When were you with Ma Rainey? Oh boy, that was when I, well I'll tell how this worked. Now Ma Rainey joined the Mac and Mac show, singing the blues, took her for the blues singer. And that's how I worked with her. When she got her own show, you know, late on I didn't work with her, I was still on the show. But I played with her with Mac and Mac.
And when you worked with Jelly Roll, would you work all year round?

Well, I didn't work with him but one year. Jelly got down sick or something, and the next year, I don't know, even Bain had this winter part, you know. And Swayze, he taken sick and died. And that was one of Jelly boozing him in, you know. And the other deal was blown in Chicago, playing different spots all around like that. So that's how I let this happen. Jelly just passed out like that, and he died pretty soon. I believe he died in New York though. Didn't die in Chicago, died in New York. But now to tell the truth about that, that was one other, I didn't say I got much money, is that they were out of a bid, but that was the coolest and the easiest job I ever had. How's that? Well, I tell how it was. When we hit a town, we'd go to work at eight o'clock. And we'd work full numbers, take off about ten minutes. We'd go back and work for four more numbers, take off ten minutes. Then we have an hour and a mission, and we'd go back for another half and half and all we were through. And that was every night. I'd wait with rain, you see. And boy, I thought that was mighty good. No way else I'd wait like that.
But when you worked with Jelly, was that after you went with Tiny Palm or before?
Let me get this straight. This year was before I went with Tiny.
No, it couldn't have been. It was after. Yeah, after. Because Tiny, I met them when I first
went to Chicago. Well, was it before you were with Hewitt Swift or after?

This was after Hewitt Swift. Yeah, after Hewitt. Between Tiny, then Hewitt, then Jelly Roll. That's, I think, where I think we... And who came after Jelly Roll? Well, that's when I got rid of this little Louisiana boy, you know.
I see. Well, that gives me a rough idea. Yeah. You know, I like to get the dates on it, roughly.

Now, there's one thing I've never told you about. He had a fellow named Leonard Reed. I don't know if you've ever heard of him. Can't place him now. Well, he's a show producer. He used to be a tap dancer a long time ago. Real light boy. But he got up on one of the best shows in Chicago ever was known. He was a guy named Dave, Dave, Dave, Dave, Riley, Dave Sutton. He used to be a gangster. But then how he had the swing land in Chicago. And he thought more Leonard Reed needed his own son. Leonard Reed wasn't no kin to him. But he was just crazy about Leonard Reed. And he gave Leonard Reed preference to build that show up. And if he get that show like he wanted it, he was going to let Leonard Reed take it anywhere he wanted. So Leonard Reed got that show down like he wanted and took it to New York. And that's the first chorus in my life I've ever seen get them claws, you know. Come back three times, back on the stage and dance three times. Uncores. Uncores, yeah. That's the first chorus I've ever seen do it. And there's a number one chorus in New York and number two is supposed to be hot. But these girls cleaned up for him. These girls cleaned up for him. Boy, I mean he had a chorus out of the books. Boy, them girls really could dance together. And a girl made a misstep on nothing no time. I'm telling you. And Leonard Reed, that was his name. We went to New York and worked at the Harlem Opera House. Went there for one week and stood there two months. Yeah, he stood there two months with that show. And then you know how it is in them towns. The guy get this girl over there and tell him what he'd pay off of. You know, and pay him more than Leonard. And the guy get another girl. And them girls went just like that. Different parts of the state of New York. Two of them went on over in England or somewhere. They're over there yet. Didn't got to be old women. They're over there yet. Yeah, but he had a short old boy.
Well, this must have been a while back.
Oh yeah, this was back there in the, 32, 31, 30 long in the day.
Whose band was he using?
Well, he had Francois Luziano.
Oh, I see.
Yeah, that's the band we was with.
Now.
But we had to build the band up. See, we had to put about, let's see, we had six pieces. And he put six more pieces in the band. Made a 12 piece of band. That's what we had to have.
Remember who he added?

Well, Al Wynn was one. I was one. Francois and Duke El, Duke Caston. I mean, his name is Charles Duke Caston, but we called him Duke. And he had Lawrence Brown on tenor, Robert Crowder on tenor, Fred Howard on alto and clarinet. And he had Clowns, Clowns Brown on piano. He had me, I'm trying to think of these trumpet players now. I forget that boy's name. But I mean, I mean anyhow, well, Hopkin went off with us. Hopkin and me and another little young trumpet, he's younger than us, but he could play a lot and he was, you know, using him for the high notes. And I was doing the getting off.
You named the tuba player or bass player?
Oh yeah, William Hillion. Same guy, huh? Yeah, he was the tuba player.
I have to play that record for you sometime.
Yeah.
Golden Lily and somebody stole my gas.
Well, Duke Caston was on guitar.
Did they have mixed bands down here when you were playing in the twenties?
White in color?
Mm-hmm. No, they didn't.
You didn't know? I didn't remember that.
You don't remember any white boys that ever sat in with you and anything? Well, yeah.

They had a boy named Jogan Duffy. Well, he couldn't play that, you know, but he would learn how to play trumpets. You know, I'd make him sit right side of me in the band and play along with me and dance and things, you know. But Joe never did learn I don't think. I haven't seen him since I left, since I've been back. I know he's an old man like I am now. See I was so good with him because he'd follow us everywhere, everywhere we went. Joe would go and his dad had a big market out there on Chippewa and something out there in front of town. And I never had to worry about no, you know, meats and things. I would go out there and get my meats and things, the time I got ready. That boy was crazy about me and I liked him. Joe Gondolfi, I never would get him.
Many other guys like that, did you remember all of them?
He's about the only one I remember. Goldeir has a lot more of them, but.
He's the only one whose name you can remember.
And he'd go around and get up dances for me. At the Italian Hall and Espinade and Ramport. All the dances I played there he got them for me.
You ever have any battles of music down here? Shucks.
I won two cups out of three.
Yeah?

With who? I won one from Chris Kelley. That's up. Tuxedo beat me. And I won one from Rene. But me and Rene split even. I'll tell you how that come out. See my bunch gave me the cup the first time we played, and then Rene had a white bunch too you see, and they gave him the cup the next time, well he and him split even see. But I won Chris Kelley and I won one from Rene and I lose with their tuxedo. They had twelve pieces and we had six. I couldn't do nothing but lose that.
I'd really have the six myself.

I ain't that little boy what you hear I'm talking about now, on drums with me. He was tying it up then. Chani. Chani was a whopping good little drummer then. That boy could play some drum. But he just was always wild, you know. But he always listened to me. He got bad after I left, you know, after I cut out and left, then he turned out bad, you know. But I could tell him, I said, Chani, we're going up to Audubon to play tonight or something like that. I said, we're not going up there drinking. We're going to go up there and play music. That's all. Okay, well he comes and he's over the land. Never did be drunk when I asked. When he started getting drunk we all were drinking, you know. That's when he started drinking.
Now, in Chicago you named several fellas that used to sit in with you, white guys. Do you remember Muggsy Spaniel? Oh sure.

Every weekend we'd do breakfast dance there, you know. And a lot of white boys come up there, gangs of them. You know, they used to come in, sit down, blowin' all of them. Limpinico, Louis Primo. All them fellas used to come up there. Louis Primo was very young then though. He was kind of a young kid, you know.
Do you remember Bud Freeman? Sure.
Yes, sure. Where did you know him?
Well, I met him.
He's from St. Louis, ain't he?
No, he's from Chicago. He played around New York, too.

But I heard he was from St. Louis, Bud Freeman, I know him, played tenor. Mustache. Yeah, I know him, but I heard he was from St. Louis. I don't know where he's from, but I heard that. He's a bad man too, partner.
You know a bass player named Jim Lanagan? Jim Lanagan.
I don't believe, that name sounds familiar, but I don't know him.
What about George Wettland and Davey Tuff, those guys?
George who?
Wettland, he's a drummer.
I don't know him, white boy. Dave Tuff.
I just wanted to do some of the ones who came around and sat in.

Well, there's so many of them, Dick, I'm telling you, he used to pile in there, man. Of course I tell you what made these to come there, see. Like, take the movie stars like George Ralph, and Harry James, and all them fellas, you know, they'd be in town playing a theater or something, and that breakfast man, they'd be there that morning. And they'd all the people that's come see them, meet them, you know. That's why that happened. Now, I tell you a lady, let's used to be with us, just as regular as we had finger to the toe, and she got to be a big star, Martha Ray.
She'd come to the Golden Leather?

Sure, Martha Ray was dead, it was the regular as that finger to her, get right down that mic and go to singing. She could sing too, partner. And first thing I know, that woman was gone, to California. I said, what's been happening here now? I said, man, they're going into business. Show the real picture. I said, well, I betcha, maybe I know she wouldn't know nothing about me. And I tell you, girl, we started out with us, couldn't sing one song. She gives our name June Richmond now. But her first name is Burdette Richmond. That's her name, Burdette Richmond, because the fella used to sing with us named Ed Goodbar, her mother was his wife. And he brought her up there, brought the girl up there to wake up with us. Said she want to be a song, and we're going to make her learn. And she learned right there with us at the Golden Leather, and got famous right there with us, partner, and hit the road. She first went out with Jimmy Wade. She went on the road with Jimmy Wade. She was a stout girl then, getting started, started. And after Jimmy Wade went back to Chicago and broke up or something like that, next time I heard a boy that, but it was in California.
What about Jimmy Wade? Did you work with him?
Oh man, yeah, a long time. Made records with Jimmy Wade.
I knew you made the records, but I didn't know you played trumpets with him.

Yeah, I played trumpet with him. That's where the woman liked to shot him down there one night. Really? Shot right through his coat and shirt right there. Well the blue singer, I forget her name. I'll tell you, her name was Ethel Cross. Ethel Cross. She was singing with me, she was a fool, you know. And they got to messing around with some other gal and they show them, she had a little automatic man. Shot right at him, shot right at home through there, that's who there. Another boy grabbed her, grabbed her hand. She was about to kill her.
This happened right in Detroit.
Right in Detroit. So you were on the road with him, son? Yeah, we was on the road.
Playing theater. How big a band did he play?
I'll tell you who was with us. Now you believe this is a lie, in the hand of Jesus. Clarence Muse, the man in pictures, he was on the show with us.
What was he doing? Singing.

Never forget the song he's singing. I laughed the day she said she'd leave, I laughed and said I wouldn't grieve. After my laughers came tears, that was his song. Who was in the band other than you and Wade? Oh Lord man, that's 12 years old.
I was in the band. I was in the band.

I was in the band. I was in the band. I was in the band. I was in the band. I was in the band. I was in the band. I was in the band. I was in the band. About My Laughers Came Tears, that was his Song.
Who was in the band other than you and Wade?

Oh Lord man, there's a 14-piece band. I swear I can't think of stuff like the names of the guys on it. Some good solo. Well I'll tell you what I wish, I wish that they'd like to do it now, put all them guys' names on the records. Oh yeah. But they don't

do that anymore. They got your book. That's what we're doing, we're working on that book, you know, the guy that put the book out, it's a friend of mine, he lives in Slidell. We're working on all that. Let me see now, did you ever work with B-Rod? No. Never did, huh?
No. We were really nice together, but I never did play with him. Did Sid Ann any with him?
No. I just thought maybe you knew some of the different guys that worked with him. No,

see he always worked at Spanish Food, that's where he always worked. And we never did go out there, we went to Millenburg, pretty like that, but I never did go to Spanish Food. I don't know, you don't even know the place where he worked at out there. Did you ever work with B-Rod? Yeah. How'd that happen? You mean, playing in the band with him? Well no, we made records on one side, he made them on the other side, but we were always in the same building, in New York, when I made it in Mexico with Edwin Hall. Yeah. Where Mutt was on, putting Mutt on one side and me on the other. And that was all made about the- See when I come in, Mutt just had left. That's how I got with his brother Jack Carey. Yeah. I see. Did you know Mutt down here at all? No, I didn't know him here, I met him up there.
Met him in New York or in California? No, New York. I see. Did you ever know Richard M Jones?

Yeah, I made records with him. Richard M Jones, crippled fellow. Yeah, played piano. Where did you make the records with him? And John had none of them records? Man, I made plenty of records with Richard M Jones. No, I don't have any of the ones you made with him. Mr. Bill didn't have none? He probably does, somewhere hidden. He must be got them records. Man, all his own stuff though, you know, he was writing out his stuff himself, you know. He could write out some nice stuff boy, Richard M Jones. Yeah, crippled fellow. I worked with him in Chicago.
You played jobs with him, spot jobs? Yeah, but you know, not gigs I mean, not going to run one steady job. You remember he was in the band with you with Richard M Jones,
either tuned or? Boy, them things would get me, look like my mind
Yeah. I'd come left over that, you know. Well, by what time was that when you were working

with Richard M Jones? Well, this was near a time when I was fixing to leave Chicago. A little time before I joined them shows, you know, and cut out of Chicago. A little before that, I was working on that way with him. Did you know a white guy named Phil Featheringale up there? Featheringale, I heard of that name many times, but I don't believe I knew him. Yeah. Yeah.
I'm trying to figure out which records you made, you know, and all that. Because I know you made some records for one of those companies. I think it was a Session company or something.
Session, yeah. That was downtown Chicago. Yeah, but that's the guy I said went away, and I never could get no royalties or nothing from him.
That must be Phil Feathering. Yeah, yeah. And those are the same ones with Richard M. Jones? Or was that...
I don't believe.
No.
I'll be to some other company. I know it was because we went to different places to make them records.

Well, hold a minute and see if I can find this book. And this was Richard M. Jones you made records with just before you left Chicago. Yeah. And you don't remember the guys in the band or anything yet?
No, that's what I asked you. I thought the name was in there.
Well, let's see. Do these tunes sound familiar now? West End Blues?
Yeah, yeah.
That's right. Boy in the Boat?
Yeah.
Sugarfoot Stomp? That's right. Muscle Shoals Blues?
That's right. I played them with him.
And that's with Richard M. Jones? That's right. The band is called Punch Miller Stompers.
Yeah.
I got the Charles Zaloni new hot discography. I looked it up.
Well, he must have been no reason for him.
Well, let's see. Artie Stalk on clarinet?
Yeah, that's right. That's right.
Who did he work with, Artie Stalk?
Well, he just was a fellow along there working with different bands and things.
Yeah, I mean, you didn't work with him much.
No, he didn't play in my band.
And Johnny Lindsay on bass?
Yeah.
Did you work with him much in Chicago?
No. Just made records, I think.
And Snaggs Jones? Yeah. I guess you didn't work with Johnny Lindsay too much down here either, huh?

I didn't work with none, yeah. He played with Robichaud the whole time he was here. And let me see how he did that. Didn't he get off a bass on trombone or a trombone on bass or something? Yeah, that's right. Something like that, I remember.
He played trombone with P. Ron.
Yeah.
And he played bass in Chicago a lot. Yeah. Played bass with Jelly Roll.
Mm-hmm.
And it seems to me he played bass down here with a band that Clarence Williams had in charge.
That was what Matthews did too. Matthews used to be a drummer. Bill Matthews.
How did he rate the drummers?
Well, he played with the tuxedos all the time. I never found out much about him.
Who were some of the good trombone players down here when you were young?

Morris French, Kid Ory, Jack Keran, and let's see who else I can... Who was with Buddy Petit? Morris French was with Rene. I'm trying to... Oh, yeah, a little boy, George Washington. He never did come back. Little bit of fella. Played nice trombone.
What happened to him?
And they had another bad man, Willie Umford's brother, Earl Umford. He was bad.
What happened to George Washington?
I don't know. That family ain't ever come back.
And who were some of the good drummers in those days?
Little Happy, you know. Chinese.
Which Happy now? We gotta get to...
Red Happy. I don't know his last name. We used to call him Red Happy.
Well, that's good enough. There's so many Happys.
And Little Chinese. Black Benny was kind of rated up there among them, too.
For what? For bass snare?
Well, I mean, he played traps and bass drum, but he's the best on bass drum. But, I mean, he played traps, too, pretty nice. And this Martin fellow, what's his name?
Henry Martin.
Henry Martin.
Albert Henry, I forget. Just a couple of Martin guys. Which one was this, the one?
The drummer, Henry Martin.
And who did he work with?
He worked with Maple Leaf or something kind of leaf band or something.
It wasn't Fats, Martin. No, no, no. Fats was another.
He was named Henry Martin. He worked mostly, though, with the Silver Leaf or the Maple Leaf or something or another.
I see. And who'd be good on snare on the street?
Snare?
On the snare drum. On the street.

Them times? Mm-hmm. I'll tell you. Henry Martin was one of the best. Mm-hmm. Well, Happy, I don't believe I've never seen him play. Yeah, I did see him play parade. He played parade with us once. Long time ago. He played nice. I had Black Benny on the bass drum. He's the bad man on the bass drum. Boy, he played more bass drum. Sure.
Now, back to the piano players. What about Manuel Bonetta? Did you ever work with him?
Yeah. Like, we'd go up to the Audubon, Turon, places like that where they'd need piano players. He'd play with us up there. He was a real good piano player. But otherwise, we didn't use no piano.
Now, who were some of the good piano players in either solo or band that you'd say were really outstanding here?

Well, Dick, that's what I'm trying to tell you. We didn't use none. And it was very similar. I was around in it to find out who was the good. Now, the one I really choose was really good. And I heard him a lot of times. And that was Steve Lewis. See? Because I heard him a lot.
Well, I don't hear any arguments on him, man.
Huh?
I don't hear any arguments on him. Everybody who listens to him hears the records. I think he's wonderful.
Yeah. Yeah, Lewis is good.
